title: Constant-round MIS in the congested clique
formal: Does randomized maximal independent set admit a constant-round algorithm in the unicast Congested Clique? Precisely, for every fixed integer \(c\ge1\), do there exist a uniform randomized distributed algorithm \(A_c\) and positive constants \(R_c,B_c\) such that, on every simple undirected graph \(G\) with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\ge2\), the algorithm always terminates within \(R_c\) rounds, uses at most \(B_c\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\) bits per directed communication link per round, and outputs a maximal independent set with probability at least \(1-n^{-c}\)? Constants and program may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\), the graph or its maximum degree.
why: The question measures how much communication exact distributed symmetry breaking needs when every processor can directly contact every other processor. A constant-round solution would establish a sharp capability of this widely studied model. A general lower bound would expose a bandwidth limitation that survives unrestricted local computation and arbitrary global coordination.
definitions: There is one processor for each vertex \(v\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Initially it knows \(n\), its own identifier \(v\), the common identifier set, and exactly the identifiers of its neighbors in the input graph. The physical communication network is complete: in each synchronous round every processor may send a separate message to every other processor, even when the corresponding input edge is absent. Messages sent in a round arrive by its end. Each directed link has the stated bit limit independently; processors may send different messages to different recipients. No extra processors or initially centralized graph description are provided. All processors run the same finite program, with their identifier and local input as parameters. Local computation and local storage have no asymptotic bound, but each local computation terminates and reads only finitely many independent private fair random bits on every execution. All communication, including initialization and distribution of any shared randomness, counts toward the round bound. No graph-dependent or size-dependent advice is supplied. At termination each processor outputs one bit, defining \(S=\{v:\text{processor }v\text{ outputs }1\}\). Correctness means both \(\forall\{u,v\}\in E(G):\{u,v\}\nsubseteq S\) and \(\forall v\notin S:\exists u\in S:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\). Thus maximality means that no additional vertex can be inserted while preserving independence; maximum cardinality is not required. The probability refers to the single global event that all output bits together define a valid set. The round and message bounds hold on every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. Restricting the requested fixed failure exponent to positive integers is equivalent to allowing every fixed positive real exponent.

progress.text: Ghaffari, Gouleakis, Konrad, Mitrović and Rubinfeld give the general \(O(\log\log\Delta)\)-round Congested Clique MIS bound; the checked arXiv version was revised in 2022.
Cambus, Kuhn, Pai and Uitto publish a constant-round Congested Clique algorithm for 2-ruling sets.
Censor-Hillel, Even, Flin and Halldórsson state the general constant-round question and prove constant-round results under restrictions on average degree and independence parameters.

status_note: The February 2025 source explicitly leaves constant-round randomized MIS on arbitrary graphs open. Its positive results concern restricted graph classes and its negative results concern specified procedures. The bounded later-work search through 2026-09-15 found no resolution of the exact model and probability target here; this is not an exhaustive certification of present openness.

context_blocks.text: The checked 2025 paper explicitly identifies constant-round MIS on arbitrary graphs as open. It records the general randomized upper bound \(O(1+\log\log(\Delta+2))\), where \(\Delta\) is the input graph’s maximum degree. The harmless offsets cover small degrees.

The 2025 result gives constant rounds on several substantial graph classes. One guarantee applies whenever average degree is at most \(2^{K\sqrt{\log n}}\) for a fixed constant \(K\); the running-time constant may depend on this fixed class parameter. These restricted guarantees leave arbitrary graphs outside their scope.

Section 5 of that paper exhibits limitations of the sampling procedures analyzed there. These are restrictions on those procedures and do not constitute a lower bound for all algorithms in the communication model of this card.

A 2-ruling set is independent and places each vertex within graph distance at most two of the selected set. The 2023 constant-round algorithm for this relaxation allows distance two, whereas MIS requires every unselected vertex to have a selected neighbor.

review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-15; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked construction and proof of the quantified algorithmic statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. A positive answer must cover every input graph and every requested fixed failure exponent with the uniformity, bandwidth and worst-case round bounds specified above. A negative answer must rule out the entire stated randomized algorithm class; a limitation of a particular algorithm family, of deterministic algorithms alone, or of broadcast communication is insufficient. Computing an independent set whose distance-two neighborhoods cover the graph does not fulfill maximal independence.

importance.reason: Asks whether all-to-all communication suffices for constant-round symmetry breaking, sharply testing the congested-clique model.

category_assignment.reason: Mapped from the existing subject category

sentences: A maximal independent set contains no adjacent selected vertices and gives every unselected vertex a selected neighbor.
Each processor starts with its own incident input edges and can send separate short messages to every other processor.
The target is a uniform randomized algorithm using a constant number of rounds on every graph.
Its output must be globally correct with an arbitrarily requested fixed polynomially small failure probability.
The checked literature gives constant rounds for restricted graph classes and for distance-two coverage, leaving the general MIS target unresolved.
